name: The Dooars & Siliguri
tagline: Rhinos, tea gardens and the gates of Bhutan
meta_description: Plan the Dooars on a budget: Gorumara and Jaldapara rhinos, Buxa Fort, Jayanti, Samsing tea slopes and Jhalong, with real costs, routes and closure dates.
summary: The Dooars are the forested plains and foothills below Bhutan in Jalpaiguri and Alipurduar districts, reached from Siliguri in two to five hours. Come from November to March for one-horned rhinos in Gorumara and Jaldapara, gaur at Chapramari, the walk to Buxa Fort and river valleys at Samsing and Jhalong.

story.title: The doors to Bhutan
paras: Dooars, or Duars, comes from the word for doors or gateways. The name meant the passes through which trade and armies moved between the Bengal and Assam plains and the hills of Bhutan; there were eighteen of them by the usual count, eleven on the Bengal side and seven in Assam. For two centuries Bhutan held the strip of plains and forest below those passes, and the Koch kings of Cooch Behar and the Raikats of Baikunthapur contested it.

The British ended that contest by force. After a diplomatic mission to Bhutan went badly in 1864, they fought the Duar War of 1864–65, captured forts such as Buxa and Daling, and under the Treaty of Sinchula, signed on 11 November 1865, annexed the Duars in return for an annual payment to Bhutan. In 1869 the western part was joined to Jalpaiguri to form a new district, and its forests were reserved for timber.

Then came tea. The first Dooars garden opened at Gazaldoba in 1874, and within decades gardens ran the length of the foothills, worked by families recruited from Chota Nagpur and the Nepal hills, with a railway to carry the leaf out. What forest was left became the parks of today: Jaldapara from 1941, Gorumara from 1949 and Buxa Tiger Reserve from 1983. Alipurduar became its own district in 2014.

intro: The Dooars are the low country at the foot of the eastern Himalaya, between the Teesta and the Sankosh, where tea gardens, rivers and sal forest share a plain that is rarely more than 100 m above sea level. Most travellers rush through on the way to Darjeeling or Sikkim. Stop, and you find India's second rhino stronghold, gaur herds at forest waterholes, a Bhutanese fort turned British prison and long white riverbeds under the Bhutan hills.

It is also one of the cheapest wildlife regions in India. Homestays in Lataguri, Samsing, Buxa and Jayanti charge ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals; forest corporation cottages cost ₹1,800–4,000 a room; safari jeeps are shared between six. Trains on the Dooars line run from NJP through Malbazar, Chalsa, Madarihat and Hasimara to Alipurduar for very little.

Siliguri is the gateway: NJP station and Bagdogra airport are minutes apart, and cars, buses and trains fan out east from here. A four-night trip covers Gorumara and Jaldapara; seven to nine nights add the river valleys of Samsing and Jhalong and the forests of Buxa and Jayanti. Parks close for the monsoon, roughly 16 June to 15 September.

highlights.title: Rhinos in Jaldapara and Gorumara
highlights.text: Around 330 one-horned rhinos in Jaldapara and about 60 in Gorumara, by the March 2025 count. Jeep safaris in Jaldapara's tall grass and watchtowers in Gorumara give two very different ways to see them.

highlights.title: Gaur at Chapramari
highlights.text: A small sanctuary with one watchtower over a forest waterhole, where some of the largest gaur herds in West Bengal come to drink in the late afternoon. Elephants come too.

highlights.title: The walk to Buxa Fort
highlights.text: Five kilometres on a stone path through forest to a fort that guarded a Bhutanese pass, held Indian revolutionaries in the 1930s and sheltered Tibetan monks after 1959.

highlights.title: Samsing and Suntalekhola
highlights.text: Tea slopes at 900 m on the edge of Neora Valley National Park, a hanging bridge over the orange stream and the Murti's boulders at Rocky Island, an hour from the parks.

highlights.title: Jhalong and Bindu
highlights.text: The Jaldhaka valley on the Bhutan border, with river birds on the shingle, a hydel town, cardamom farms and the last Indian village at the end of the road.

highlights.title: Jayanti and Mahakal
highlights.text: A huge pale riverbed below the Bhutan hills, a long walk to a limestone cave revered as Shiva's shrine, and evenings when elephants cross the river.

getting_there: Fly to Bagdogra (IXB) or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), the railhead for the whole region. From there, reserved cars cost about ₹3,000–3,500 to Lataguri or Murti (75–85 km, two to two and a half hours), ₹3,500–4,500 to Samsing, ₹4,000–5,000 to Madarihat for Jaldapara (125 km, about four hours) and ₹5,500–6,500 to Jayanti or the Buxa road head. Buses from the Tenzing Norgay terminus in Siliguri run east towards Malbazar, Birpara and Alipurduar for ₹100–300. The cheapest and most pleasant option is often the train: Dooars line services run from NJP and Siliguri Junction to New Mal Junction, Chalsa, Madarihat, Hasimara, Rajabhatkhawa and Alipurduar, but timetables change, so check before you plan. Shared jeeps run up to Samsing and Jhalong from Chalsa, mostly in the morning.
permits: Indian citizens need no special permit for the Dooars. Every national park and sanctuary charges entry, vehicle, guide and camera fees, and safaris must be booked through the West Bengal forest department, online or at counters in Lataguri, Madarihat and Rajabhatkhawa; carry the ID used to book. Foreign nationals pay higher fees and should carry passports, especially near the Bhutan border at Jhalong, Bindu, Totopara and Buxa. There are no border crossings for travellers in the parks; entry to Bhutan is via Phuentsholing opposite Jaigaon, with Bhutan's own documents and fees. Rules change: check current status before you travel.
money: A shoestring day in the Dooars costs about ₹1,800–2,500 per person: a homestay with dinner and breakfast at ₹1,200–1,800, a shared seat in a safari jeep at ₹450–700, trains and buses between towns and a dhaba lunch. A comfortable day, with forest corporation cottages or a resort, a reserved car and private safari jeeps, runs ₹4,000–6,500. People overspend in three places: hiring a car for the whole trip when trains and buses would do between bases, booking safari jeeps for two people instead of sharing, and paying resort prices in Lataguri for a room they only sleep in. Book safaris online early; last-minute counter seats often go to agents.

months.summary: The coldest and clearest month. Mornings in open safari jeeps are cold and often foggy until 8 am, but grass has been cut and burned and rhinos are easy to see. Migratory ducks fill the Gajoldoba barrage near Siliguri. Hills at Samsing and Jhalong drop to around 6–8 °C at night. Weekends around New Year are busy, the rest of the month calmer.
months.tip: Pack a warm jacket and a scarf for 6 am safaris; open jeeps are colder than the thermometer suggests.

months.summary: Perhaps the best all-round month: warm afternoons, clear mornings, short grass and good rhino and gaur sightings. Maha Shivaratri often falls in February, bringing the Jalpesh Mela near Maynaguri and pilgrims to the Mahakal cave at Jayanti. Paths to Buxa Fort and Lepchakha are dry and views over the plains still clear.
months.tip: If Shivaratri falls on your dates, book Jayanti homestays early or base yourself in Rajabhatkhawa.

months.summary: Animals come out to the drying waterholes and salt licks, which makes March excellent for gaur at Chapramari and rhinos at Gorumara's towers. Days warm up and haze begins to soften views from Lepchakha. Tea gardens start the first flush. Shivaratri sometimes falls in early March. The rhino census usually takes place in early March, when some areas may close briefly.
months.tip: Take the last afternoon slot for gaur at the Chapramari waterhole.

months.summary: Hot and humid on the plains, with thunderstorms building in the afternoons. Parks remain open and wildlife viewing at water is good, but midday is uncomfortable. The hills at Samsing, Suntalekhola and Jhalong are pleasant and green, and the tea gardens are busy with plucking. Prices fall after the winter rush.
months.tip: Plan safaris for dawn and dusk and spend the hot hours in the hills or by a river.

months.summary: Pre-monsoon showers grow heavier and leeches appear on forest paths. Parks are open until mid-June, and animals are still active early and late. It is a good month for tea gardens in full flush and for cheaper rooms, but not for long walks. River camps begin to close as the rains near.
months.tip: Carry a rain layer and keep a buffer day; storms can cut power and delay trains.

months.summary: The monsoon arrives and the national parks and sanctuaries close from about 16 June. Rivers rise quickly, and roads to Samsing, Jhalong and Bindu see slides. Siliguri carries on normally. We do not plan Dooars trips for June, except for tea garden stays for travellers who want rain and green above everything else.
months.tip: If you must come, see Gorumara and Jaldapara in the first two weeks before closure.

months.summary: The heart of the monsoon. Parks are closed, riverbeds at Murti, Jayanti and Bindu are full and dangerous, and roads into the hills are unreliable. Tea gardens are at their greenest, and Shravan brings pilgrims to the Jalpesh temple. Homestays that stay open offer low rates.
months.tip: Keep away from riverbeds entirely; water levels change within minutes after rain in the hills.

months.summary: Still deep monsoon, with parks closed and frequent floods. Karam is celebrated in many tea gardens in August or September by Adivasi families whose ancestors came from Chota Nagpur. It is a community festival; join only if a host invites you. Otherwise, save the Dooars for later.
months.tip: Visit tea garden communities only with an invitation and travel in daylight.

months.summary: Rain continues through most of the month and parks reopen from about 16 September, though grass is tall and sightings harder. Karam may fall in September. Late-month weekends can be good value for tea garden homestays. Check current status before you travel, since floods and repairs can delay reopening.
months.tip: If parks have just reopened, choose watchtowers over jeep routes; grass hides animals.

months.summary: The rains end and the Durga Puja and Diwali holidays bring huge crowds from Bengal, so book lodges and safaris early. Grass is still tall in Jaldapara, and some routes may be closed after monsoon damage. Late rain is possible; in October 2025 extreme rain caused severe floods. The hills are clear and green.
months.tip: Avoid the Puja week unless you have bookings; prices and crowds peak.

months.summary: One of the best months: dry, sunny days, cool mornings, clear views over the plains from Buxa and Lepchakha, and parks fully open. Grass is cut back through the month, improving sightings. Migratory birds return to rivers and the Gajoldoba barrage. Weekends are busy, weekdays pleasantly quiet.
months.tip: Book Jaldapara and Gorumara slots online as soon as your dates are fixed.

months.summary: Cool, dry and clear, with foggy mornings on the plains and crisp days in the hills. Rhino and gaur sightings are good, river birding at Jhalong and Murti is at its peak and the riverbeds are wide and dry. Christmas and New Year weeks are crowded and expensive; early December is ideal.
months.tip: Trains through the Dooars can run late in winter fog; allow slack for connections at NJP.

faqs.a: Dooars, or Duars, means doors or gateways. It refers to the passes from the Bengal and Assam plains into Bhutan, eighteen by the usual count, and to the strip of plains and forest below them. Bhutan held this land until the British annexed it after the Duar War of 1864–65.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit the Dooars?
faqs.a: November to March, when parks are open, days are dry and grass is short enough for good sightings. February and early March are especially good. October and April are acceptable. Parks close from about 16 June to 15 September for the monsoon.

faqs.q: How many days do we need for the Dooars?
faqs.a: Four nights cover Gorumara and Jaldapara: two in Lataguri or Murti, two in Madarihat. Six or seven nights add Samsing or Jhalong and Buxa. Nine nights let you see almost everything, from Siliguri to Jayanti, at an easy pace.

faqs.q: How do I book safaris in Gorumara and Jaldapara?
faqs.a: Through the West Bengal forest department's online booking system, as soon as your dates are fixed; winter weekends sell out. Leftover seats are sold at counters in Lataguri and Madarihat. Bring the ID used to book. A six-seat jeep with fees costs roughly ₹2,500–4,000.

faqs.q: How much does a Dooars trip cost?
faqs.a: About ₹1,800–2,500 per person a day on a shoestring with homestays, shared jeeps and trains; ₹2,500–4,000 with forest corporation cottages and some private cars; ₹4,000–6,500 with resorts and a car throughout. A four-night value trip from NJP costs around ₹13,000–15,000 per person.

faqs.q: Is Hollong lodge in Jaldapara open?
faqs.a: Hollong, the wooden forest lodge inside Jaldapara, was gutted by fire on 18 June 2024. We have not confirmed that it has reopened. Stay at Madarihat instead, and check with the forest department before booking anything advertised under the Hollong name.

faqs.q: Did the October 2025 floods affect the Dooars?
faqs.a: Yes. Extreme rain in early October 2025 flooded the Torsa, Jaldhaka, Murti and other rivers, killing wildlife in Gorumara and Jaldapara and damaging roads and bridges. Parks closed for a time and reopened after repairs. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Dooars good for families with children?
faqs.a: Very good. Drives from NJP are two to four hours, safaris are short, the Medla bullock-cart ride and Dhupjhora's elephants delight children, and homestays welcome families. Keep children away from riverbeds after rain and inside compounds after dark.

faqs.q: Can we visit Bhutan from the Dooars?
faqs.a: Yes, via Jaigaon and Phuentsholing, about 20 km from Hasimara, with the documents and fees Bhutan currently requires. There are no border crossings for travellers at Jhalong, Bindu, Buxa or Jayanti, even though Bhutan is across the river.

to_confirm: Hollong forest lodge, Jaldapara: gutted by fire on 18 June 2024 (not 2025, as the brief suggested); rebuilding was discussed but reopening is unconfirmed. Content presents it as closed.
October 2025 floods: Jaldapara was shut indefinitely in early October 2025 and Gorumara lost wildlife; exact reopening dates and any routes still closed need checking.
Monsoon closure dates for all parks (16 June – 15 September) and 2025–26 safari fees, jeep rates and elephant safari status at Jaldapara and Dhupjhora are indicative and need current confirmation.
Rhino figures from the March 2025 estimate (Jaldapara about 331, Gorumara about 61) are taken from news reports of the forest department count; confirm against the official report.
Gorumara national park date: Wikipedia gives 31 January 1992 (some sources say 1994). Jaldapara national park status: 2014 per Wikipedia (some sources say 2012).
Gorumara as the best-managed protected area of 2009 (Ministry of Environment and Forests) is from Wikipedia; confirm wording.
Chapramari train accident: seven elephants killed in November 2013 on the Dooars line; confirm date and exact location.
Jalpesh temple: attribution to Koch kings and later Raikat rebuilding varies by source; dates deliberately left vague.
Buxa: Tagore's 1931 poem and the detainees' greetings for his 70th birthday are recorded on the fort memorial; confirm wording before quoting.
Mahakal cave walk distance (about 5–6 km each way) and Pokhri lake route/time are from local accounts and vary; confirm with Jayanti guides.
Jaldhaka hydel project: begun in the 1960s with Bindu barrage feeding Jhalong; exact commissioning year and capacity not stated.
Distances Jhalong–Bindu (10–15 km), Lepchakha above Buxa (about 4–5 km) and Totopara from Madarihat (about 22 km) are approximate.
